items.title: Generalist Action Critic: Harnessing Frontier Models in Autonomous Driving

evidence.quote: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC) , a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models’ general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR’s HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.

items.title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization

evidence.quote: To answer these questions, we present Meta-RTL , which evolves an RTL optimization harness from a minimal seed through two nested loops. In the inner loop, a fixed LLM optimizes RTL designs under the current harness. In the outer loop, a proposer LLM improves the harness much as an engineer would: it traces EDA failures in the inner-loop logs back to specific harness decisions, hypothesizes a targeted fix and its expected effect, probes the fix on a few relevant designs, and revises it based on the evidence. Each submitted harness is then frozen and scored on all development designs by synthesis and equivalence checking outside its control. In this way, EDA feedback improves not only the designs but also the harness that produces them. While skill libraries capture what transformations to apply, Meta-RTL learns how to search for effective transformations, turning a traditionally hand-designed process into an optimization target.

An archive 𝒜 \mathcal{A} stores harness implementations, evaluation results, and execution trajectories. Harnesses are ranked by normalized timing–area utility Q ⁡ ( H ) Q(H) (Section III-D ), and the highest-scoring eligible harness, Meta-RTL ∗ , is selected and then evaluated on unseen designs.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Self-supervised Vision Backbones Survives Distribution Shift in Radar Micro-Doppler HAR

evidence.quote: Micro-Doppler radar enables contactless, privacy-preserving human activity recognition (HAR), but deployment robustness remains underexplored. We compared full fine-tuning, frozen probing, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) using subject-disjoint in-distribution cross-validation and few-shot cross-age, cross-orientation, and cross-dataset transfer. Full fine-tuning suffered negative cross-dataset transfer, while frozen features under-adapted on cross-orientation. Only PEFT avoided both failures. We paired DINOv3 with all-layer principal-singular-direction adaptation (PiSSA), to our knowledge the first application of a self-supervised image foundation backbone to radar micro-Doppler HAR. DINOv3-PiSSA ranked first among PEFT methods in every evaluated setting. Under our protocol, its Small variant matched the in-distribution accuracy of the prior Base-size PEFT state of the art using 4.5 × 4.5\times fewer total parameters, with only 3% trainable. It surpassed a size-matched variant of that baseline in every evaluated setting, with transfer gains increasing with shift severity: 2.1, 6.6, and 8.9 percentage points, respectively. Ablations attributed improvements to both pretraining and adapter recipe, with the pretraining contributing most under compound shift. Code and protocol are available at https://github.com/KeryanChelouche/udoppler-ssl .

items.title: Harnessing Medical Visual-Language Models with Agentic Evidence Management

evidence.quote: Medical vision–language agents increasingly rely on segmentation tools, and recent work has focused on acquiring the right mask, often treating a good mask as the end point of tool use. However, do these tool-augmented agents actually make effective use of the evidence once it is obtained? To answer this question, we need a benchmark that separates evidence use from segmentation quality, spans multiple medical image types, and allows the same mask to be presented in different ways. Existing medical VQA datasets do not jointly provide these properties. We therefore construct Mask-Evidence MedVQA , a 2.5K-example benchmark spanning four image types, where each question is paired with an answer-relevant ground-truth mask and multiple possible renderings. Our study reveals two limitations of direct tool use. First, evidence presentation matters. Different renderings of the same fixed mask can substantially change model behavior. Second, masks introduce an evidence trade-off . Highlighting a relevant region can expose diagnostic evidence the model previously missed, but the added visual cue can also induce incorrect associations. As a result, even a ground-truth mask can correct some answers while turning initially correct ones into incorrect ones. Together, these findings show that acquiring the right mask is not enough; an agent must also decide how to present the evidence and whether it should change the answer. We therefore introduce TUNE ( T ool U se is N ot E nough) , an evidence-management harness that explicitly manages what evidence to acquire, how to present it, and whether to accept the resulting answer update. Across three public medical VQA benchmarks, evidence management improves the fine-tuned Qwen3.5-9B backbone’s mean accuracy by 4.0 percentage points. Full TUNE improves over direct tool use by 9.1 points on average across seven benchmarks and achieves competitive results against existing medical VLMs and agents.

items.title: HapBO: Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors

evidence.quote: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed α \alpha - π \pi Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ( π : 𝒳 → [ 0 , 1 ] \pi:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1] ), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on α \alpha - π \pi BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6–15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12–20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

items.title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses

evidence.quote: Team-based modification turns the feedback of a round into generalizable harness changes through four roles that collaborate in the Gitea repository. Triage filters issues and keeps the requirements worth pursuing. The Architect finds requirements that share a root cause and merges them into one structural requirement. The PM finds requirements that users leave unstated across sessions and writes them as product requirements documents (PRDs). The Developers write a design document called a request for comments (RFC) for each admitted requirement or PRD and then open a PR to implement it. Triage and the Architect handle the issues that users file, and the PM handles the user ratings and summaries of sessions. The two routes run in parallel, and their output reaches the Developers only through admission (Section 3.3 ).

Requirement-driven selection merges only changes that resolve a verified requirement and pass review. It applies two gates. The first is admission, which passes only requirements and PRDs backed by session evidence to the Developers. The second is review, which merges a PR only after its RFC passes design review and its code passes code review against the acceptance criteria of the RFC.

Before implementation, a design review checks that the RFC preserves the objective, intervenes at the layer that owns the behavior, covers interface and state boundaries, and specifies a test that could falsify the design, and a failed check sends the RFC back for one revision. After implementation, a code review checks the PR against the acceptance criteria of the RFC, requires the full test suite to finish, and returns PASS or REWORK, and REWORK sends the PR back to the Developers. A PR merges into the main branch only when the approval is bound to the current head of the PR and the RFC still matches the reviewed design, and the merge closes the requirement or PRD that the PR implements. Every change is a git commit, so the Developers can revert any change during review and conflict resolution.

items.title: Harnesses That Improve Themselves: A Unifying Framework for Self-Improving Agent Harnesses

evidence.quote: How an agent harness connects the model to the environment. In a long-horizon task, a frozen foundation model cannot inspect a workspace, execute commands, or track multi-step state on its own. Instead, it operates inside an executable agent harness (such as Claude Code, Antigravity, Mini-SWE-Agent, or Terminus) that mediates interaction with the live environment across every turn (Fig. 1 , left) [ 4 , 8 ] . Unlike a static prompt template, the harness governs autonomous execution across dozens or hundreds of turns through four coupled, code-editable components. First, Context and State Management controls multi-turn history across the trajectory by assembling dynamic instructions, separating working memory from experiential memory [ 31 ] , and masking or compacting stale observations across prior turns so long horizons do not overflow context [ 32 , 33 ] . Second, Agent Control steers multi-turn exploration by regulating turn budgets, detecting and breaking repetitive loops, switching between planning and execution phases, and delegating subtasks to isolated subagents [ 8 , 25 ] . Third, the Action Interface defines how the agent acts upon the environment through an Agent-Computer Interface (ACI) [ 2 , 34 ] , translating model outputs into sandboxed shell commands [ 35 ] , file edits, or GUI actions while parsing or truncating single-turn raw stdout and UI state on the current step and loading tool schemas on demand [ 36 ] . Fourth, Verification and Recovery intercepts stop or state-commit signals from Agent Control to run automated test suites, linters, or visual checks, routing failures back into Context and State for self-repair before termination [ 37 , 38 , 39 ] . Fine-grained modular systems further split these four components into five modules (separating single-turn observation formatting from multi-turn context management [ 25 ] ) or four lifecycle contexts (plan, supervise, verify, recover [ 39 ] ), while pre-execution action guards bridge Component 3 and Component 4 [ 40 ] .

The four-stage closed-loop self-improvement cycle. Because these four runtime components interact tightly across a trajectory, a flaw in one component quickly cascades into others. Self-improving harness frameworks replace manual debugging of these coupled components with an automated outer loop (Fig. 1 , right) that iteratively evolves the harness over successive rounds. In Stage 1 (Diagnose Failures), the system runs the current harness on a development split to collect multi-turn rollout trajectories, and localizes systematic harness bottlenecks by clustering verifier errors, diffing passing and failing trajectories, or searching raw execution logs [ 19 , 8 , 21 ] . In Stage 2 (Propose Edits), an optimizer translates these diagnostic findings into concrete code or hook patches across one or more harness components [ 25 , 22 ] . In Stage 3 (Validate and Filter), candidate harnesses are screened on validation tasks, trace-replay simulators, or efficiency frontiers to check runtime execution, prevent regressions, and filter out overfitted or token-wasteful edits [ 20 , 24 , 41 , 42 ] . Finally, in Stage 4 (Deploy or Route), a validated patch is either merged into the default harness for subsequent runs [ 19 , 8 ] , saved to an archive of harness variants that future search rounds can branch from [ 29 , 24 ] , or paired with a lightweight router or policy that selects a tailored harness configuration for each incoming task [ 43 , 44 ] .

Zero-shot transfer to a stronger model. When transferred without re-tuning to Gemini 4 Argon (Table IV , Part B), compact code mechanisms generalize far better than long, uncompacted horizons. On the seed harness, Argon avoids empty-diff exits through stronger instruction following, yet still burns all 12 turns reading uncompacted files and solves only 10.0 % 10.0\% of held-out tasks. Prompt-Only Reflection reaches 15.0 % 15.0\% . Unconstrained Full-Harness Rewrite drops to 30.0 % 30.0\% , as Argon’s longer reasoning chains compound with 28 turns of uncompacted context. Modular Gated Evolution achieves the highest accuracy on both repositories ( 37.5 % 37.5\% overall) at 64.8 ​ k 64.8\text{k} tokens per task, beating the unconstrained rewrite at less than one-fourth the token cost.

We never update the model weights or train a value critic: the harness is the only part of the policy that changes (§ 2 ). We implement this approach in GUARD ( Grader-free UED with Adaptive Rule Distillation ; Figure 2 , § 4 ). items.title: How Feedback-Free Self-Evolution Reshapes Agent Skills: A Systematic Study

evidence.quote: Feedback-free self-evolution. Each model rewrites a skill from its text and a one-sentence topic, with an instruction to identify problems and improve the skill. We provide no task, outcome or judgment. Each rewrite replaces its predecessor for thirty recursive rounds to trace where repeated rewriting leads. The same model then uses its rewritten skills as an agent, giving rewriting an opportunity to adapt the skill to that model.

Our analyses show performance declining as skills lose content outside the model’s prior. To further test whether this association reflects a causal relationship, we restore original skill items lost during rewriting and measure task performance. Starting with skills after thirty successive rewrites, we remove conflicting versions of lost items to form a common base. We restore the original items, producing one version with items outside the prior and another with the other lost items. We evaluate agents with both versions on all three benchmarks. On SkillsBench, restoring the items outside the prior recovers most of the lost pass rate, about twice as much as restoring the other items, and restoring all lost items recovers about as much as restoring these alone, although it puts back more text. Losing the knowledge outside the prior therefore causes much of the decline. The value of an expert’s skill lies largely in this knowledge, which is exactly what rewriting without feedback gives up first.

The value of an expert’s skill lies largely in the knowledge outside the model’s prior. Without feedback, a rewrite cannot add this knowledge, since the skill is its only source, and can at best keep it. The original skill already holds it, so what remains is whether the agent uses it. An agent may pass over these items when it follows a skill and fall back on what it would do by itself, much as a rewrite falls back on what the model would write. We therefore propose SkillDiff, a simple method that improves a skill without feedback and without changing its text, by finding the items outside the model’s prior and pointing the agent to them.

items.title: TRACE: Attribute Execution for Sequential Image Editing

evidence.quote: Given an image and successive user instructions, sequential image editing should return an updated image that satisfies each new request and preserves earlier requirements that remain active. This lets users develop a result without repeatedly restating or repairing their decisions. The difficulty is that a retrieved image can contain a valid color on an obsolete surface, while the current image may lack the newly requested material. Neither reference selection nor a precise object mask alone specifies how to reconcile attributes occupying the same region. We present TRACE, which separates the continuing attribute from its visual carrier and prioritizes local appearance operations under complete-request checks. Active-goal binding identifies what should persist, carrier selection supplies suitable current or newly generated pixels, and tonal calibration reduces tinting near highlights and shadows. Experiments across frozen editors, independent visual readers, new source images, and complete sequential benchmarks support joint color–material recovery and show how local execution preserves the surrounding scene.

items.title: Context as a Resource

evidence.quote: Managing concurrent tasks across separate agent sessions quickly exhausts human attention, motivating always-on personal agents behind a single continuous interface. Yet when every context shares identical frozen backbone weights, funneling interleaved dialogues and external events into one linear session induces cross-topic constraint bleed and head-of-line stalling. Conversely, router–ticket hierarchies incur lossy prose handoffs, heavy routing overhead, and blind merges—collapsing true-conflict repository merges to a 33.3 % 33.3\% three-run mean despite high isolated branch passes. Rather than scheduling anthropomorphic roles, we introduce ClonAct , a routerless architecture that virtualizes context blocks directly through a pluggable single-pass non-generative Context MMU, in-place Context Cells, a footprint-aware Synaptic Bus with an isolated trial merge gate, and a wave-flushed Shared Trunk. Across three programmatic multi-stream benchmarks and three model families, our portable trial merge gate lifts true-conflict merges to 63.3 % 63.3\% , while ClonAct ’s routerless virtualization attains this ceiling with 45.9 % 45.9\% fewer prompt tokens and prevents compact-model router collapse. Under continuous surge streams, ClonAct matches top completion ( 95.0 % 95.0\% ) with the lowest median wait and zero timed-out status checks.

items.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming

evidence.quote: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network’s weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84–17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83–110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23–14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

items.title: DACA: Dual-Anchor Collaborative Agent for Zero-Shot 3D Visual Grounding

evidence.quote: 3D visual grounding (3D-VG) is a task that bridges the natural language and 3D space, serving as a foundational capability for embodied intelligence and human-computer interaction. Although recent 3D-VG agents overcome the reliance on pre-processed 3D point clouds, they essentially employ a unidirectional, pipeline-style tool-calling architecture. This architecture separates semantic understanding from geometric reconstruction, leading to error accumulation and an inability to autonomously recover from failures. To address this flaw, this paper proposes the D ual- A nchor C ollaborative A gent (DACA), which reinterprets 3D-VG as a semantic-geometric dual-anchor collaborative reasoning paradigm. DACA comprises two complementary specialized tools: the semantic anchor tool holds the visual semantic features of the target and achieves efficient target tracking via optical flow and VLM local verification; the geometric anchor tool holds the 3D spatial geometric features of the target and performs global spatial reasoning via voxelization and multi-keypoint projection. The two components exchange information bidirectionally via a standardized tool call protocol, autonomously deciding on the next perception-action step to form a closed-loop optimization. Experiments on the ScanRefer and Nr3D benchmarks demonstrate that zero-shot DACA achieves an overall Acc@0.25 of 73.6% on ScanRefer and 70.4% overall accuracy on Nr3D, far surpassing the latest zero-shot 3D-VG methods. The code and models are available at https://github.com/liujia99/DACA .

items.title: HabitusMem: Belief Memory over Evolving User Preferences for LLM Agents

evidence.quote: Personalized LLM agents must act on a user’s current preferences, which change across interactions and are rarely stated in full. Existing memory systems store and retrieve content from the interaction history and leave the agent to work out which preferences still hold and where they apply. Such content does not indicate whether a preference is still current or where it applies, so agents often act on outdated or misapplied preferences. We instead treat memory as the assistant’s belief about the user. Following Bourdieu’s account of habitus as durable but revisable dispositions, we model the user as a latent preference state that every interaction, including the current request, both reveals and updates. The belief summarizes what the history supports about this state, and memory consists of the individual beliefs that bear on the agent’s current decision, each with its evidence, scope, and status. We implement this view in HabitusMem, a trained writer that states these beliefs as text records for a frozen agent. Across two agent families, HabitusMem achieves the best results among memory systems on both PersonaMem-v2 and VitaBench 2.0. Controlled analyses show that learned request conditioning drives the answering gain, while auxiliary training tasks improve tool use.

items.title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents

evidence.quote: Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action–observation interactions. items.title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading

evidence.quote: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading , a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

items.title: SCAFFOLD: Toward Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport for Reusable LLM-Agent Skills

evidence.quote: Abstract—An agent skill that succeeded yesterday may be executable today without being justified for reuse today. Tests may cover only observable contract clauses, outcome oracles may be absent, evaluations may inherit the same erroneous specification, and permissions or dependencies may change between validation and invocation. We argue that the appropriate unit of prospective trust is a Warranted Reuse Claim (WRC): a defeasible, claim-specific authorization tied to a versioned skill, target context, evidence, assumptions, and identified defeaters. The paper sharpens this position through Warrant-Preserving Evidence Transport (WPET), a proposed discipline for deciding which historical evidence remains admissible after context change. evidence.quote: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. items.title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception

evidence.quote: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA) , a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent’s upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent’s decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.

items.title: Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents: State-Transfer Auditing and Controls in the Agent Harness

evidence.quote: This paper presents a state-transfer audit architecture across four harness stores:

The harness moves state across these stores. Observations bring environment state into the context, and context assembly loads workspace rule files, tool schemas, and retrieved memories. Compaction moves older turns to session history and leaves a condensed summary or placeholder (which page back can later reload on demand); memory writes and consolidation extract and merge entries from the working context or session history across runs. Actions change the environment, and rollback restores prior state across the environment, working context, session history, persistent memory, and inference-server KV cache. Multi-agent harnesses add delegation , which passes a task and state slice to a sub-agent with its own context. Each transfer gives the harness a concrete boundary to record and check what crosses.

Long-horizon LLM agents across codebases, web browsers, and enterprise infrastructure rely on an execution harness to move state between the working context, session history, persistent memory, and external environment. While conventional execution traces log model prompts and tool calls, critical security and reliability failures occur during state transfers: a transfer can admit unchecked content (indirect prompt injections, unverified memory writes), rewrite state lossily (context compaction dropping user constraints, memory consolidation stripping source authority), or restore state incompletely (workspace rollbacks leaving aborted KV state active on the inference server). Because current traces omit what crosses these boundaries, failure attribution and runtime monitors fail on multi-step trajectories. We present a state-transfer audit architecture for the agent harness. At each transfer boundary, we define an audit point specifying the minimal hash-chained record the harness emits, separating low-overhead deterministic checks from model-based semantic checks and binding internal context, memory, and inference-server cache state to external actions. We show that the same transfer records required for causal failure attribution supply the durable state needed by runtime security controls, including least-privilege capabilities, replay-resistant authorization outside the prompt, information flow control, obligation monitors, and transactional recovery across multi-agent and infrastructure pipelines. Finally, we analyze multimodal GUI adaptations and implement and evaluate a reference harness middleware across 240 multi-step fault-injection trajectories, showing that transfer records localize root causes and catch cross-transfer violations missed by lifecycle and tool-only logs at microsecond deterministic overhead.
